title: Lecture 4. Models of Prevention
summary:
📋 Main Lecture Topics
  1. Biomedical Model of Prevention
  2. Model of Chronic Disease Prevention
  3. Comparison of Infectious and Chronic Disease Prevention Models

Previous sessions discussed the differences between models of infectious and chronic diseases, the concept of stress as a general predictor of deviant behavior, and the concept of factors—direct causes of stress and behavioral deviations. In this session, we will try to generalize all this knowledge into a model for preventing deviant behavior.

Let's recall that, in a broad sense, prevention refers to any actions aimed at reducing the likelihood of an undesirable phenomenon occurring, as well as reducing the severity of its development and negative consequences.

1. Biomedical Model of Prevention The biomedical model of prevention stems from the infectious disease model, which was discussed in a previous session. It is built on simple logic and addresses three categories of people:

  • Primary prevention is aimed at preventing the onset of disease. Its main target is healthy people who have not yet been infected with anything. They are vaccinated, sanitary norms are developed for them and they are taught to observe them to avoid infection, wash hands before eating, eliminate possible foci of diseases, and increase resistance (resilience) to possible illness. In the current era of the coronavirus pandemic, requirements for wearing masks, hand sanitization, and restrictions on visiting various public places have emerged. (The goals of primary prevention in the biomedical sense also include: the damaging agent (infection), routes of infection transmission, and impact on the human body to strengthen its resistance to disease. However, discussing these details is beyond the scope of this course).
  • Secondary prevention is aimed at preventing the worsening and chronification of a condition when early symptoms of a disease appear. That is, the secondary link of prevention targets people with signs of disease or those with a diagnosis made by a doctor. Such individuals are identified through screening measures, such as medical check-ups. As we recall, infectious diseases typically have clear criteria for the presence of pathology, which can be identified, for example, through tests, by detecting a specific pathogen.
  • Tertiary prevention, also called rehabilitation, is aimed at preventing exacerbations of a past illness and relapses, reducing the negative consequences of the disease, and restoring bodily functions. Thus, its target is people who have overcome the acute phase of the disease and are already in remission.

It should be noted that for a number of diseases, the role of a psychologist in tertiary prevention is important, particularly concerning addictive states. The most striking example is addictive behavior. It is quite easy to make a person stop using alcohol and drugs and undergo detoxification. And periodically, severe drug addicts themselves come for treatment to reduce at least the dose, not at all intending to quit. Like any alcoholic's dream – to learn to drink without binges. Every alcoholic wants to recover in such a way as to continue drinking. But the question is: how to make addicts who want to recover resistant to relapses? And here, unfortunately, there are no medical measures to prevent cravings, although attempts have been made to create them. There is no such serum or injection that would make one lose the desire to play cards or roulette. And so, psychological intervention methods must be used at the tertiary prevention stage. Not because it's necessary, but simply because there's nothing else to do.

Traditionally, the role of patient behavior in these three links of prevention was practically not considered. It was believed that treatment consisted of purely medical procedures implemented only under the supervision of a doctor. However, in the case of diseases and disorders where a behavioral component is important, the simple and logical biomedical model proved to be largely unsuitable, for reasons already discussed in previous sessions. But the main one is that chronic diseases do not have clear criteria for the onset of the disease; they are characterized by a long "pre-disease" period. Consequently, the criteria for transitioning from primary to secondary prevention are unclear. Psychiatrists who dealt with the treatment of behavioral disorders have long substantiated the need for a prevention model that would detail the initial phases of the disease.

2. Model of Chronic Disease Prevention For the reasons mentioned above, a model for the prevention of mental illnesses was developed in the 1980s, which subsequently gained recognition for many other behavioral disorders as well. Unlike the biomedical model, it details the primary prevention link – emphasizing "pre-disease" states and the important role of human behavior in the formation of illness (Gordon, R. (1983) An Operational Classification of Disease Prevention. Public Health Reports, 98, 107-109). This model was the result of a long discussion among many clinicians in American psychiatric periodicals. Today, methodological documents of the World Health Organization dedicated to the prevention of negative phenomena in adolescent behavior, such as drug addiction, suicidal behavior, etc., are based on this model.

The model includes three links of prevention (which, according to many authors, collectively belong to the primary prevention link in a general medical sense). Applied to the topic of adolescent deviance, the model is as follows.

Universal prevention is aimed at the entire adolescent and youth subpopulation and can set its goals as: forming motivation for a healthy lifestyle, strengthening mental health, informing about the harm of certain types of "risk" behavior, shaping media policy in public health, increasing trust in professional help in the field of physical and mental health, etc. This is the most non-specific link of prevention, meaning it is not tied to a specific problem but is aimed at building resilience to health risks in general.

Selective prevention is addressed to representatives of "risk" groups characterized by a high level of experienced stress, but without specific signs of any behavioral disorder. In other words, their high level of stress can manifest in various deviations. Such risk groups may include, for example:

students on internal school records or registered with the Juvenile Affairs Commission (KDN), children who have experienced trauma or abuse, children with a high level of neuropsychic tension, adolescents who identify with certain counter-cultures, adolescents likely using alcohol and tobacco, students with low academic performance, children from migrant families, etc. Selective prevention, unlike universal prevention, targets specific risk groups within the youth and adolescent subpopulation. The idea of selective prevention is that "risk" behavior primarily results from psychological or life problems that an adolescent cannot cope with independently. In this context, behavioral disorders are an indicator of a high level of stress. Thus, the goal of selective prevention is the early identification of an adolescent's psychological or life problems and the provision of professional help before they lead to serious behavioral disorders.

Indicated prevention targets vulnerable groups or individuals not just with a high level of stress, but with specific signs of a particular behavioral disorder. Its purpose is the early identification of individuals with pronounced signs of "risk" behavior and the timely provision of professional help, primarily psychological.

It is important to emphasize that indicated prevention, unlike the previous links, targets representatives of risk groups who have pronounced signs of behavioral disorders but do not yet have the status of patients from a medical point of view. Such individuals may include, for example, drug users who do not have clinical signs of drug addiction, from a doctor's perspective. They are not included in the statistics of the sick, but for them, form No. 37 "Information on patients suffering from alcoholism, drug addiction, substance abuse" provides a section — "Preventive registration."

Adolescents falling into this prevention link may exhibit characteristic changes: a sharp decline in academic performance, narrowing of interests, indifference or, conversely, aggression towards parents, loss of interest in their usual circle of friends and social environment, alcohol and toxic excesses, etc. Such young people often come to specialists or preventive programs not on their own – they are brought by parents, friends, or referred by education system workers or law enforcement agencies. This important observation highlights the fact that young people themselves at this stage often already feel "excluded" from society. Their social environment and the specialists carrying out preventive measures require special efforts to foster motivation for a full life in the young person. Unlike selective prevention, the goal of individual prevention is not just short-term socio-psychological behavioral correction, but involving the adolescent in long-term work that includes a comprehensive analysis of various aspects of their life and work with their immediate social environment – parents, siblings, and significant peers. Such a work strategy in education system documents is usually called individual preventive work (IPR). More details about its possible technologies will be discussed in the second module of the course.

3. Comparison of Infectious and Chronic Disease Prevention Models

3. Comparison of Infectious and Chronic Disease Prevention Models

Correlation of Prevention Model Links

Prevention of INFECTIOUS diseases Prevention of CHRONIC diseases
Primary prevention entire population or youth subpopulation, no symptoms or patient status Universal prevention entire population or youth subpopulation Selective prevention risk groups, with generally high stress levels Indicated prevention individual representatives of risk groups, with specific signs of behavioral disorder
Secondary prevention symptoms and diagnosis present, made by a doctor
Tertiary prevention rehabilitation after recovery or overcoming the acute stage of illness

 

Thus, a prevention model is necessary to optimally focus available resources on solving a particular problem. Let's summarize the concepts studied in this course module in a table comparing the logic of infectious and chronic disease prevention.

Model of INFECTIOUS disease prevention Model of CHRONIC disease prevention
Source of the problem Infection Stress
Manifestations and consequences Medical symptoms Behavioral disorders (deviance)
Causes of the problem (factors) Identify the pathogen using tests or a doctor's examination Select and test theories of deviance using socio-psychological research methods
Identify target groups for prevention Medical criteria Behavioral (demographic, social, psychological) criteria
Choose prevention methods targeting significant problem factors Specific treatment, e.g., medication for a specific infectious agent Mainly non-specific ways to reduce stress levels.
